newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: China says non-interference key to Australia ties.
newsitem.headline: China says non-interference key to Australia ties.

text.p: Chinese Vice-Premier and economic tsar Zhu Rongji said on Wednesday "mutual non-interference" was necessary for continued harmonious relations between China and Australia.
Speaking to the Australia China Business Council, Zhu said relations were good, but warned that China and Australia should "agree to disagree".

"Though our two countries differ in social system and values, the level of economic development, culture, tradition and historical development, we should respect...each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity and mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs," Zhu said.
"On this basis we will be able to steadily develop our bilateral ties in a sustainable manner," he said.
Australia-China relations chilled last year over a series of diplomatic and security spats, with Beijing expressing concern over Australia's closer military ties with the United States.
But on Wednesday Zhu dismissed any concern about Australia's security pact with the United States.
"There has existed traditional friendship between our two peoples and neither of us poses any threat to the other," Zhu said.
Zhu's week-long visit to Australia, which has attracted small human rights protests in Adelaide and Sydney, is seen by Australia as an opportunity to improve ties.

Zhu told Beijing-based Australian reporters last week that he had cancelled a European tour and opted to visit Australia as a payback for Australia abandoning a U.N. resolution censuring China over its human rights record.
Australia dropped its opposition in favour of formal human rights dialogue with China, which will begin in August.

China is Australia's fifth largest trade partner, with two-way trade worth A$8 billion (US$5.3 billion) in 1996. Trade is growing about 20 percent a year and China is projected to move to Australia's number two trade partner by 2005.
